subject: ISLAMIC RELIGIOUS EDUCATION
title: Children’s Obligations to Other Family Members
overview: A Muslim family is wider than mother, father and children. Grandparents, brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts and cousins are also family. In this sub-strand you will name those members, learn a child's duties towards them, and see why keeping the family bond is an act of ibadah.

lessons.title: Other family members and our duties to them
objectives: Name members of the extended family.
Outline a child's obligations to those family members.
lessons.intro: When relatives gather for a wedding, aqiqah or a visit, you meet people who share your grandparents even if they do not live in your house. Islam calls you to know them and to treat them well.
lessons.notes:
### Who the other family members are
Besides parents, a child's family includes:

- Brothers and sisters
- Grandfathers and grandmothers
- Uncles and aunts, on both the father's side and the mother's side
- Cousins
- Other close relatives the family keeps in touch with

These relatives are often called the extended family. In many homes a grandparent or an uncle also helps to raise the children. They are still part of this duty.

### Obligations of children
The learning in this sub-strand names practical duties. They are acts of ibadah when done to please Allah:

- Respect: greet elders first, use polite titles, and do not laugh at their age or their way of speaking.
- Visiting: go with your parents to see relatives, especially the sick and the elderly. Do not wait only for parties.
- Attending ceremonies: join family events such as a wedding, aqiqah or a funeral gathering in the way your parents guide you. Be helpful and well behaved there.
- Helping: carry a chair, serve a drink, look after smaller cousins, or assist a grandparent with a simple task.
- Caring: ask how they are, make dua for the sick, and share what you have when you visit.

### A chart of names
Knowing names is part of the bond. A child who can say "This is my maternal aunt" and "These are my cousins" is ready to keep the tie. Write the names your parents allow you to record. Do not invent relatives, and do not share private family matters in class.

keyWords.meaning: relatives beyond parents and children, such as grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins
worship; a good deed done to please Allah

examples.problem: Sort these people into 'parents' and 'other family members': mother, cousin, father, grandmother, uncle, sister.
steps: The others are family members this sub-strand is about. A sister is part of the household and is also among the relatives a child must respect and help.
examples.answer: Parents: mother, father. Other family members: cousin, grandmother, uncle, sister.

activity.title: Extended family chart
steps: In groups, draw a simple chart with spaces for grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts, brothers, sisters and cousins.
Each learner adds the names of extended family members that he or she may share in class.
Under the chart, write the obligations: respect, visiting, attending ceremonies, helping and caring.
Hang the chart where the class can see it, and one learner explains it.

practice.question: Name four members of the extended family.
practice.answer: Any four: grandfather, grandmother, uncle, aunt, cousin, and other close relatives. Brothers and sisters may also be named.

practice.question: State the five kinds of obligation named for children towards other family members.
practice.answer: Respect, visiting, attending ceremonies, helping and caring for them.

practice.question: What is the difference between a maternal aunt and a paternal aunt?
practice.answer: A maternal aunt is a sister of one's mother. A paternal aunt is a sister of one's father.

practice.question: How can helping at a family ceremony be an act of ibadah?
practice.answer: When it is done to please Allah and to keep good family ties.

summary: Other family members include siblings, grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins.
Children respect them, visit them, attend family ceremonies, and help and care for them.
These duties are ibadah when done to please Allah.

lessons.title: Why the family bond matters
objectives: Explain the significance of fulfilling obligations to other family members.
State how a Muslim keeps the bond even when relatives live far away.
lessons.intro: A rope is strong when every strand is held. Family ties are like that. Islam does not want the strands to be cut.
lessons.notes:
### Keeping ties of kinship
The Prophet (S.A.W) said that whoever would like his provision to be increased and his life to be extended should uphold the ties of kinship (Bukhari). Keeping the bond is called silat al-rahim. Cutting it, without a right cause, is a serious wrong.

Allah commands believers to be careful about family ties. A Muslim does good to relatives because Allah ordered it, not only because they gave a gift last year.

### Why these obligations matter
- They please Allah and are rewarded as ibadah.
- Relatives support one another in sickness, poverty, celebrations and grief.
- Children learn manners, history and faith from grandparents and older relatives.
- Visits and ceremonies stop the family from becoming strangers.
- Respect for elders spreads peace in the home and in the wider community. This is social cohesion: people relate well instead of quarrelling.
- A child who keeps family ties is practising for good citizenship, because the same respect is later shown to neighbours and the community.

### When relatives are far
Distance does not cancel the duty. A family can send salaam through a parent, make dua, share news, and visit when travel is possible. If a relative is unkind, the Prophet's teaching is still to keep the tie in a good way and not to reply to harm with worse harm. Children follow their parents' guidance on visits and do not go to relatives' homes alone without permission.

Appreciating the bond means you are glad to belong to these people, you speak well of them, and you do not gossip about family matters.

keyWords.meaning: keeping the ties of kinship with relatives
the relationship among members of a family
people living together in peace and good relationship

examples.problem: Hawa's grandmother lives in another town. Hawa says, "I cannot visit every week, so I have no duty." What is wrong with this idea, and what can she do?
steps: Distance reduces visits; it does not end silat al-rahim.
She can send salaam, make dua, and visit when the family travels.
examples.answer: The duty remains. She should keep the bond through salaam, dua and visits when they are possible.

activity.title: Why we keep the bond
steps: In pairs, brainstorm the significance of fulfilling obligations to other family members.
Write at least four points, including one benefit to the child and one benefit to the whole family.
Discuss one way to keep the bond when a relative lives far away.
Present your points and listen to the other pairs without interrupting.

practice.question: What is silat al-rahim?
practice.answer: Keeping the ties of kinship with relatives.

practice.question: Give three reasons why fulfilling duties to other family members is important.
practice.answer: Any three: it pleases Allah; relatives support one another; children learn from elders; the family does not become strangers; it spreads peace.

practice.question: What did the Prophet (S.A.W) connect with upholding ties of kinship?
practice.answer: He said that whoever would like his provision to be increased and his life extended should uphold the ties of kinship.

practice.question: Name two ways to keep a family bond when relatives live far away.
practice.answer: Any two: send salaam, make dua, share news through parents, visit when travel is possible.

summary: Silat al-rahim means keeping ties with relatives, and it pleases Allah.
The bond brings help, learning and peace.
Distance does not cancel the duty.

lessons.title: Practising good relationship with the family
objectives: Demonstrate obligations to other family members in short scenes.
Choose ways to maintain the family bond.
lessons.intro: A visit can strengthen a family or embarrass it. The difference is in the greeting, the help you offer, and the way you speak.
lessons.notes:
### How to behave with relatives
- Greet the oldest person first, with Assalamu alaikum, and shake hands or respond in the way your family teaches.
- Sit where you are asked to sit. Do not push cousins aside for the best place.
- Offer help before you are begged: pass plates, fetch water, or keep younger children from the cooking area if an adult asks.
- Listen when an elder is speaking. Do not correct an elder rudely, and do not whisper and laugh about them.
- At a ceremony, follow the programme. Do not wander off, demand money, or use a phone to record people without permission.
- If a grandparent is ill, a short quiet visit, a dua and a small service are better than a noisy crowd.
- Thank the hosts before you leave.

### Building the habit
Choose one relative to remember this month. It may be a grandparent or an aunt. Ask your parent the best way to show care: a visit, a drawn card with salaam, or help on a family day. Do that one thing. Then keep it up.

Good relationship is not only receiving gifts on Eid. It is also being present, useful and polite. When children do this, adults are encouraged to keep the same bond, and the family stays joined. That is the appreciation this sub-strand asks for: valuing the relatives Allah has given you and maintaining the tie.

keyWords.meaning: the celebration and sacrifice for a newborn, held in the way the family observes
the person whose home or event you are visiting
an older relative who should be greeted and listened to with respect

examples.problem: At an uncle's house, two cousins start a loud argument over a chair while adults are talking. What should a dutiful child do?
steps: The noise disrespects the elders and the host.
A dutiful child stops the fight, offers to share or take another seat, and apologises if needed.
examples.answer: Quiet the argument, give way on the chair, and show respect to the adults in the room.

activity.title: Drama: a family visit
materials: A few chairs set out as a relative's sitting room
steps: In groups, prepare a short play of a visit to a grandparent or an uncle.
Include a greeting, an offer of help, polite listening, and a goodbye.
Present the play. The class points out the obligations that were shown.
Each learner writes one action he or she will take this month to maintain a family bond.

practice.question: Whom should you greet first when you enter a room of relatives?
practice.answer: The oldest person, or the elders, with Assalamu alaikum.

practice.question: Give three good manners during a family visit or ceremony.
practice.answer: Any three: greet elders, sit where you are asked, offer help, listen, do not record people without permission, thank the host.

practice.question: Why is a family bond not only about receiving gifts?
practice.answer: It is also about being present, useful and polite, and about keeping the tie to please Allah.

summary: Greet elders, help hosts, and listen during visits and ceremonies.
One real act of care is better than many unused promises.
Maintaining the bond is how a child appreciates the family Allah has given.

quiz.question: Which of these is an extended family member?
quiz.explanation: An uncle is a relative. Classmates and workers are not family by that fact alone.

quiz.question: A paternal aunt is…
quiz.explanation: Paternal means related through the father.

quiz.question: Which set matches the obligations in this sub-strand?
quiz.explanation: Children respect relatives, visit them, attend ceremonies, and help and care for them.

quiz.question: When can helping at a family aqiqah be ibadah?
options: it is done to please Allah
it is done to show off
it is done while insulting cousins
quiz.explanation: Intention turns a family duty into worship.

quiz.question: Silat al-rahim means…
quiz.explanation: The phrase names the Islamic duty of maintaining family ties.

quiz.question: Give one benefit of fulfilling obligations to other family members.
quiz.answer: Any one: it pleases Allah; relatives help one another; children learn from elders; the family stays close; it spreads peace.
quiz.explanation: The bond serves both worship and family life.

quiz.question: The Prophet (S.A.W) linked upholding kinship ties to which of these?
options: provision being increased and life being extended
quiz.explanation: This is the well-known Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari.

quiz.question: A grandmother lives far away. How does a child maintain the bond?
options: sending salaam, making dua and visiting when the family can
quiz.explanation: Distance changes the method, not the duty.

quiz.question: At a relative's house the dutiful child…
options: pushes to get the best chair
greets the elders and offers help
quiz.explanation: Greeting and helping are practical signs of respect.

quiz.question: Appreciating the family bond means…
quiz.answer: Valuing relatives and keeping the tie through respect, visits, help and good speech.
quiz.explanation: Appreciation is shown by maintaining the relationship.
